title: A Radiators for the Interior
premise: After her mother Ruth's funeral, Kestrel Ishikawa returns to the family house in the fading coastal town of Marrow Bay to sort the estate before its scheduled demolition. Behind a bedroom wardrobe she finds a box of letters—decades of correspondence her mother wrote and never sent—to a woman named Odile, whose existence Kestrel never knew. Reading them, Kestrel discovers that her mother's lifelong silence concealed a betrayal: Ruth had testified against Odile's brother in a trial that destroyed him, out of loyalty to Kestrel's father, and spent forty years unable to choose between truth and belonging. As demolition day approaches, Kestrel tracks down Odile, now elderly and estranged, and must decide whether delivering the letters heals the past or simply redistributes its damage; the novel ends with Kestrel reading one final unsent letter aloud at the house's edge as the walls come down, choosing truth without abandoning the memory of love.
about_author: Gideon Lockridge is the pen name of a former archivist who spent twelve years cataloging unclaimed estate letters for a county records office. Their fiction explores what families preserve, discard, and refuse to say.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Three days after the funeral, she begins cataloging the house room by room, recording objects and the silences attached to them. Her careful lists are revealed as a coping mechanism for a mother who never explained anything. Emotional beat: grief expressed as control.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A certified letter confirms the house will be razed in six weeks under a redevelopment order. Her brother Theo argues to let it go quickly; Kestrel resists without knowing why. Emotional beat: the deadline becomes a character, pressing on every choice.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Moving the wardrobe to clear the bedroom, she finds a cavity in the plaster holding a shoebox: forty-one letters, all addressed to an 'Odile Vasseur,' none stamped or sent. The earliest is dated two years before Kestrel's birth. Emotional beat: vertigo—the inventory has failed her.

chapters.title: First Letter
chapters.summary: Ruth's voice via letter, framed by Kestrel's reading. The 1979 letter describes a friendship in luminous detail—Odile as Ruth's 'other interior.' Kestrel realizes her mother had a whole life she performed away from. Emotional beat: intimacy with a stranger who was her mother.

chapters.title: Theo's Version
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. When Kestrel mentions the box, Theo shuts down hard, insisting some things should stay buried with the dead. His anger hints he knows more than he admits. Emotional beat: loyalty deployed as a weapon against truth.

chapters.title: The Trial Name
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In the library archives she finds a 1981 newspaper clipping: Odile's brother Émile Vasseur convicted of arson at the cannery where Ruth and her husband worked. Ruth is listed among witnesses. Emotional beat: the silence acquires a shape and a date.

chapters.title: Letters of the Middle Years
chapters.summary: Alternating Kestrel's present with Ruth's 1980s letters. Ruth writes about watching Odile leave town, about father Henri's demands, about the baby Kestrel as 'the reason I stay quiet.' Emotional beat: sympathy complicating judgment.

chapters.title: Return to Marrow Bay
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She drives into the old cannery district, half-ruined, asking after the Vasseur name. Locals deflect; one old dockworker says only, 'You're Ruth's girl.' Emotional beat: belonging offered by strangers who knew more of her mother than she did.

chapters.title: What Theo Buried
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, flashback to 1998. Young Theo once found a single letter and confronted Ruth, who made him promise silence 'for Kestrel's sake.' He has carried the secret as his own inheritance. Emotional beat: loyalty as a burden mistaken for love.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Motel
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She confronts Theo, who finally admits he knew and begs her to stop, warning that truth will cost her the good version of their mother. They part badly. Emotional beat: siblings on opposite sides of the same grief.

chapters.title: The Address That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A tracing agency finds Odile Vasseur lived in Portland until recently; the trail ends at a care facility that denies any resident by that name. Kestrel suspects someone is shielding Odile—or Odile is shielding herself. Emotional beat: hope sharpened into obsession.

chapters.title: Émile's Grave
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. At the cemetery she finds Émile's headstone, maintained fresh for decades by an anonymous hand—cut flowers, no note. Whoever tends it is still here, still loyal. Emotional beat: evidence of devotion that outlasts justice.

chapters.title: The Gardener
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Odile. An elderly woman tends the grave; we learn she returned to Marrow Bay two years ago, knowing the house would fall, waiting for something she won't name. Emotional beat: patience as a form of accusation.

chapters.title: Recognition
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Following the gardener from the cemetery, Kestrel comes face to face with Odile, who looks at her and says, 'You have her hands.' Odile refuses to talk—but gives Kestrel a key to her late brother's storage unit. Emotional beat: shock braided with recognition.

chapters.title: Storage Unit 114
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Inside: Émile's tools, his trial transcripts, and letters HE wrote to Ruth from prison—begging her to recant, then forgiving her, then going silent. Kestrel learns the conviction may have been false and her father may have known why. Emotional beat: the floor of the story gives way.

chapters.title: Henri's Ledger
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, with transcript excerpts. Cross-referencing the trial record with her father's old work ledgers, Kestrel reconstructs it: Henri set the fire for insurance and let Émile take the blame; Ruth knew and chose her marriage over the truth. Emotional beat: horror arriving calmly, itemized.

chapters.title: Odile's Door
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile recounts, at last, the night Ruth came to her door in 1981 and said nothing—only stood there—and how that silence was worse than any confession. She tells Kestrel she doesn't want apology; she wants the letters read aloud where the house can hear. Emotional beat: grief meeting grief across the wound.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Letter forty-two, written days before Ruth's death, is different: not addressed to Odile but to Kestrel herself, hidden deepest in the box. Ruth confesses everything and asks her daughter to deliver the others—not for forgiveness, but so the silence dies with the house. Emotional beat: the mother's voice reaching through at last.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo arrives at the house intending to stop Kestrel, reads the final letter alone in the dark kitchen, and weeps for the boy he was when Ruth first bound him to silence. He calls Kestrel: 'Come home. I'll stand with you.' Emotional beat: loyalty realigned with truth.

chapters.title: Reading at the Wall
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. On demolition morning, Kestrel, Theo, and Odile gather at the property line. Kestrel reads the letters aloud in sequence as the excavators idle, giving each unsent word its audience after forty years. Odile answers each letter aloud from memory. Emotional beat: catharsis through ceremony.

chapters.title: The Walls Come Down
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The house falls; dust rises over the three witnesses. No reconciliation is tidy—Odile does not forgive, Theo does not forget—but something true has been said in the place where it went wrong. Emotional beat: release without absolution.

chapters.title: A Radiator for the Interior
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, epilogue. Months later, Kestrel donates the letters and transcripts to the county archive under both names, Ishikawa and Vasseur, so the record holds them together. She begins writing letters of her own—the sendable kind. Emotional beat: inheritance transformed from silence into speech.
